record.paper_title: Physical Layer Security in Satellite Communication: State-of-the-art and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can physical-layer security strategies be developed specifically for inter-satellite communication, including both radio-frequency and optical inter-satellite links, when such links are increasingly attackable in low-earth-orbit constellations, remain understudied in the literature, and exhibit distinctive physical-layer characteristics such as fading, Doppler shift, and weather-condition effects that may be exploitable for security, while optical inter-satellite links still lack proposed defenses against threats such as eavesdropping?

evidence.quote: There is limited focus on securing inter-satellite communications in the literature for both RF and optical links. In particular, inter-satellite links have unique physical layer characteristics in terms of fading, doppler shift, and weather condition effects that can be exploited to secure communication.

Moreover, optical inter-satellite links provide high speed and bandwidth, but it is still vulnerable to attacks such as eavesdropping, and there are no proposed solutions yet in the literature. PLS strategies are promising techniques that need to be studied extensively in inter-satellite communication scenarios by investigating their physical features and possible attacks.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation in which pairs of satellites communicate over inter-satellite links (ISLs). Two link types are present: (i) radio-frequency (RF) ISLs, modeled by a time-varying channel with parameters capturing small-scale fading, large Doppler shifts due to relative orbital motion, and atmospheric/weather-induced attenuation when links graze the atmosphere; and (ii) free-space optical (FSO) ISLs, modeled by a line-of-sight channel with pointing/acquisition/tracking errors and atmospheric turbulence effects. An eavesdropper, located either on another satellite, on an aerial platform, or on the ground, attempts to intercept the legitimate transmission without active cooperation.

Within the framework of physical-layer security (PLS), where the security metric is the achievable secrecy rate
   C_s = [ log_2(1 + SNR_legit) − log_2(1 + SNR_eve) ]^+,
formulate concrete PLS strategies (e.g., beamforming, artificial noise injection, cooperative jamming, secret key generation from reciprocal channel features, or coding schemes) that explicitly exploit the distinctive physical-layer characteristics of inter-satellite links — namely the fading statistics, Doppler shift, and weather-induced effects on RF ISLs, and the narrow-beam, turbulence-affected nature of optical ISLs — to maximize C_s (or an equivalent secrecy outage / secrecy capacity metric) against eavesdropping and related passive attacks. Provide, in particular, a defense scheme for optical inter-satellite links against eavesdropping with provable secrecy guarantees.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent surveys and research papers on satellite PLS (2023–2025) consistently identify inter-satellite link security, especially for optical ISLs, as an under-explored area with few concrete PLS schemes proposed; the problem remains broadly open, though some initial work on RF ISL secrecy and FSO eavesdropping models has appeared.

status_evidence.title: Physical Layer Security in Satellite Communication: State-of-the-art and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: There is limited focus on securing inter-satellite communications in the literature for both RF and optical links.
status_evidence.claim: Inter-satellite PLS is explicitly listed as an open problem with no proposed defenses for optical ISL eavesdropping.
